Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette: Tane grew up in a house where joy was a liability and silence was a warning. When his guardian's temper flared, the air would first fill with the acrid stench of burning wood from the stove, a smell that preceded every beating. The man's heavy boots and broad shoulders mirrored the exact physical profile of the boys Tane was forced to watch being beaten in his neighborhood, and any display of laughter or relief in those boys was met with swift, brutal correction. To Tane, the event made visceral sense: warmth signaled violence, resemblance meant danger, and happiness was a fragile illusion that guaranteed punishment. His Polynesian heritage had once anchored him in tight-knit community circles, but the abuse had stripped that foundation away, leaving him to navigate adulthood as a detective whose PCL-5 score of 62 confirmed the severe toll of his internal state. As the years passed, those early associations calcified into a relentless pattern. When the acrid scent of a nearby trash fire filled the precinct parking lot, or when a juvenile suspect bore the same jagged cheek scar as his abuser, Tane's instinct was immediate retreat; he would cancel his shifts and isolate himself from everyone around him. Those sensory flashes did not merely provoke avoidance; they cracked his mental walls wide open, dragging him backward without warning to the full, unfiltered intensity of the nights his guardian turned his anger into physical punishment. Once a memory locked in, it acted like a lens, warping his environment so that ordinary positive emotions felt dangerously out of place and anyone smiling with too much warmth became a potential threat. The sudden recall of his abuser's raised hand sent his heart hammering against his ribs, tightening his chest until his body assumed a permanent state of physical reactivity and watchfulness. As the rage on recall surged and the narrative of his childhood collapsed into untranslatable fragments, he leaned harder on detachment, forcing his mind to go numb so he could survive the shift. By actively avoiding similar clothes and pushing people away, he starved his brain of corrective experiences, which only allowed the detached memories to fester and return with sharper clarity. Every time he turned away from a crowd or changed his wardrobe to steer clear of his abuser's preferred style, he inadvertently taught his mind to scan for those exact patterns, sharpening his sensitivity to people who looked similar to the victims. Because he had come to believe his fractured worldview meant he was fundamentally broken, each intrusion felt less like a memory and more like proof that he lacked the capacity to handle his own life. When he tried to explain the abuse to his captain, losing the thread mid-sentence, he interpreted the confusion not as trauma but as character blame, cementing the conviction that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he is. This isolation bred a quiet, accumulating conviction that his avoidance proved he was a lousy coper, reinforcing the shattered beliefs that the world was inherently treacherous and his nature was fatally flawed. The relentless physical reactivity and sleep vigilance, leaving him exhausted and trembling through his rounds, convinced him he was a lousy coper who had shattered his own ability to function. As his nervous system remained permanently wired on guard, his threat monitoring expanded until even the rustle of a heavy jacket or the distant hum of a grill became a potent olfactory or visual danger cue. Now, at fifty-six, the loop had tightened enough to fracture his career and his marriage. Tane sat in his cramped apartment, the blinds drawn, still wearing the same dark, heavy canvas jacket he had bought decades ago to blend in but now refused to take off because it mirrored his abuser's preferred silhouette. He had come to seek help only because the hypervigilance had finally cost him his partner; he could no longer sit through a precinct briefing without his hands shaking or his eyes darting to the door. What frightened him most was the quiet hope that someone might help him untangle the terror he no longer understood, so he could stop treating every ordinary moment like a prelude to violence.
